questions.q: State the general outer electronic configuration of s-block, p-block, d-block, and f-block elements.
questions.a: s-block: ns¹⁻² (Groups 1–2); p-block: ns²np¹⁻⁶ (Groups 13–18); d-block: (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ns⁰⁻² (Groups 3–12); f-block: (n−2)f¹⁻¹⁴(n−1)d⁰⁻¹ns² (Lanthanoids/Actinoids). A wrong answer (e.g., writing ns²np⁶ for d-block) reveals confusion between the principal quantum number of the valence shell and the penultimate shell being filled.

questions.q: Why is helium placed in the p-block (Group 18) even though its electron configuration is 1s²?
questions.a: Helium has a completely filled valence shell (1s²) with no p orbitals in n=1. Its chemical inertness and closed-shell configuration match the noble gases (ns²np⁶ for n≥2). Placing it in Group 18 preserves the periodic trend of zero valency and high ionization enthalpy. A student who says "helium belongs to s-block because of 1s²" ignores that block classification prioritizes chemical properties over strict orbital-filling order for this exception.

questions.q: An element has the ground-state configuration [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p³. Identify its block, group, period, and atomic number.
questions.a: Last electron enters 5p → p-block. Period = highest n = 5. Group = 18 − (6 − 3) = 15 (since 5p³ means 3 electrons in p-subshell of period 5, Group 13 has 1, Group 14 has 2, Group 15 has 3). Z = 36 (Kr) + 10 (4d) + 2 (5s) + 3 (5p) = 51 (Antimony, Sb). Incorrect group (e.g., Group 5) shows misunderstanding of IUPAC 1–18 numbering versus old Roman numerals.

questions.q: Compare the valence orbital availability for the first member of a p-block group (e.g., boron) versus the second member (e.g., aluminium). How does this affect their maximum covalency?
questions.a: Boron (n=2) has only 2s and 2p orbitals (4 orbitals total) → max covalency 4 (e.g., [BF₄]⁻). Aluminium (n=3) has 3s, 3p, and empty 3d orbitals (9 orbitals) → can expand octet, max covalency 6 (e.g., [AlF₆]³⁻). A student who claims both have max covalency 4 misses the role of accessible d orbitals in periods ≥3.

questions.q: A student writes the configuration of chromium (Z=24) as [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s² and says it is a d-block element because the last electron enters 3d. Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is partially correct in block assignment (Cr is d-block) but the configuration is wrong. Actual ground state: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ due to extra stability of half-filled d-subshell. The "last electron" concept refers to the aufbau building order, not the final configuration after stability adjustments. The student confuses the filling order (4s before 3d) with the final arrangement.

questions.q: Design a mnemonic or visual scheme to remember the order of orbital filling (aufbau) for periods 4–7 that clearly shows where s, p, d, f blocks begin and end. Explain how your scheme helps predict the number of elements in each period.
questions.a: Example scheme: Write n=4 row: 4s (2) → 3d (10) → 4p (6) = 18 elements. n=5: 5s (2) → 4d (10) → 5p (6) = 18. n=6: 6s (2) → 4f (14) → 5d (10) → 6p (6) = 32. n=7: 7s (2) → 5f (14) → 6d (10) → 7p (6) = 32 (incomplete). A good scheme uses arrows or a diagonal diagram (Madelung rule) linking (n+l) values. Poor answers merely list orbitals without connecting to period length or block boundaries.
